He emphasized the critical need to move away from legacy protocols and implement systems that can be remotely controlled and updated, noting that many current traffic sensors still require physical site visits for maintenance and updates, which is inefficient and potentially insecure in modern operational environments. 1.3.2 Legacy Device Experience in AI-Driven Smart Community Control for Accelerating PV Adoption and Enhancing Grid Resilience(Rajendra Adhikari, NLR) In this talk, Rajendra Adhikari from NLR’s Building Technologies and Science group shared an overview of a Net Zero Energy (NZE) community project and the challenges that had to be addressed. Many NZE communities have a high proportion of photovoltaic (PV) generation, which can cause issues like overvoltage, voltage flickers, and degraded power factors within the electrical distribution system. Existing solutions had an insufficient understanding of behind-the-meter systems. The project team developed and validated a hierarchical community-scale solution to resolve these grid issues by connecting Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven control with a Home Energy Management System (HEMS) and an aggregator (Jin et al. 2022). In a pilot study in Basalt Vista, an affordable housing community in Basalt, Colorado, a cloud-based HEMS was deployed to manage four homes. It interfaced with a nearby energy distribution feeder, the home’s PV generation and battery storage systems, and the home’s Internet of Things (IoT) assets. A Next Unit of Computing (NUC) was deployed in each home to serve as a bridge between household and cloud. Each home was equipped with eGauge powerline adapters (eGauge 2025) to facilitate ethernet-over-powerline connections (Sagar 2011) for the home’s energy assets. Additional technology was deployed to connect legacy devices: water flow sensors to measure water consumption, copper gateways to connect the utility meters, and SkyCentrics controllers (SkyCentrics 2025) to control the water heaters. The web-based HEMS provided real-time monitoring and control for the homeowners, and AI-based autonomous control to optimize energy use. Echoing sentiments from Sanyal’s transportation presentation, Adhikari noted that real-world deployment brings new risks and challenges which cannot be anticipated or tested in a laboratory environment. While some of these challenges of field deployment could be derisked with a reconnaissance trip, it was crucial to have local personnel with site access to help solve unexpected issues. Remote access to smart plugs for power cycling and TeamViewer (TeamViewer 2025) on the NUC for monitoring and remote support were extremely helpful in addressing issues as they came up. Snowfall presented another hurdle as the snow cover on solar panel reduced generation to well below the forecast generation based on weather data. Overall, the team found that they had to balance the tradeoff between optimal grid control and homeowner satisfaction. During the discussion, Adhikari shared that building and testing the setup in a laboratory setting prior to deployment greatly sped up the field deployment. With these prior tests, local setup in the community only took one day. Utility- based control was simulated through the system, but not integrated at the time of the project.
